t: Adding Two Negabinary Numbers — Digit-by-Digit Addition with Carry
o: We must add two numbers written in base -2 (negabinary), where digit positions have values $(-2)^i$. The twist versus normal base addition is that the base is negative, so carries can be negative or require special handling. In Example 1, [1,1,1,1,1] = 11 and [1,0,1] = 5; adding gives 16 = $16\cdot(-2)^0$, which is [1,0,0,0,0]. Examples 2–3 show trivial zero handling. Constraints (lengths up to 1000) mean we cannot convert to a normal integer in fixed-width languages safely for large inputs conceptually, but the intended solution is a linear scan from least significant digits with careful carry logic.
k: Process digits from least significant to most significant, like ordinary addition, but the carry rules differ because the base is -2.

A clean carry rule: if carry is odd, emit digit 1 and set next carry to -(carry+1)/2... concretely: let s = sum of digits + carry; if s is even output 0 else output 1, then carry = -(s >> 1) using floor division toward negative infinity.
After processing all digits, strip leading zeros but keep at least one digit so zero stays as [0].

a.n: Approach 1: Convert via Python big integers (brute force)
a.i: Convert each negabinary array to an integer by evaluating $\sum d_i (-2)^{n-1-i}$, add them, then re-encode the sum back to negabinary. This works instantly in Python thanks to arbitrary precision integers, making it a great sanity-check approach.
s: Evaluate each array as an integer using Horner's rule: val = val * (-2) + digit.
Re-encode: repeatedly take n % -2 adjusted into {0,1}, divide by -2 with floor division until n becomes 0.
Handle the case where the result is 0 by returning [0].
a.t: O(n + m) per language shown — single pass over digits plus carry propagation of at most one extra digit.
a.sp: O(n + m) for the result array.

a.n: Approach 2: Direct digit-by-digit addition with floor-division carry (optimal)
a.i: Add corresponding digits plus a running carry. If the total s is even, the output digit is 0; otherwise it is 1. The next carry is $-\lfloor s/2 \rfloor$ (floor division). This works because $s = d + 2c$ implies $d = s \bmod 2$ and $c' = -(s-d)/2 = -\lfloor s/2 \rfloor$ when we write $s = d - 2c'$; the identity keeps every emitted digit in {0,1} and the carry bounded in {-1,0,1}. Note that in C++/Java/JavaScript, right shift on non-negative s equals floor division here since s >= -1 and s>>1 floors correctly for negatives too on two's-complement machines.
s: Start pointers at the last index of both arrays and carry = 0.
While any pointer is valid or carry != 0: compute s = carry + current digits.
Append s & 1 (the parity bit) to the result (least significant first).
Reverse the result and strip leading zeros, keeping one digit minimum.
a.t: O(n + m) — one pass over both arrays plus O(1) work per digit; the loop runs at most max(n,m)+2 times.
a.sp: O(n + m) — the output can be up to two digits longer than the longer input.

w: In an interview, go straight to Approach 2 after briefly mentioning why naive binary addition fails (carries behave differently with a negative base). Key pitfalls: forgetting that carry can be negative, mishandling the trailing-zero strip (must keep [0] when the answer is zero), and off-by-one errors when both arrays are exhausted but a carry remains. Edge cases: [0]+[0]=[0], results needing an extra leading digit, and cancellation producing zeros. Follow-ups: implement subtraction in negabinary, multiply two negabinary numbers, or generalize the carry formula to base -k.
